look_here_first: Start with the leaves and fruit. Mexican buckeye has alternate odd-pinnately compound leaves, usually with several broad serrate leaflets, and a distinctive three-lobed woody capsule containing large glossy dark seeds. Pink spring flowers often appear before or with the new foliage.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaves alternate, odd-pinnately compound, without stipules

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: showy pink to rose-purple spring flowers, often before full leaf-out

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: fruit a conspicuous three-lobed/three-valved woody capsule

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: large glossy dark-brown to black seeds held inside the capsule

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: not a true Aesculus buckeye despite the common name

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Alternate odd-pinnately compound leaves with opposite leaflet pairs plus a terminal leaflet; petiole base has a pulvinus.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Pink spring flowers are borne in clusters and are a useful seasonal cue, but fruit architecture is stronger for confirming the genus.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: A woody, usually three-lobed capsule that splits to expose large shiny dark seeds.

key_traits.label: Field tip
key_traits.text: Do not confuse 'Mexican buckeye' with Aesculus. Ungnadia has alternate pinnately compound leaves and a three-lobed capsule; Aesculus typically has opposite palmately compound leaves.
